newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECHS TO INTENSIFY "FINAL" GAS TALKS WITH NORWAY.
newsitem.headline: CZECHS TO INTENSIFY "FINAL" GAS TALKS WITH NORWAY.

text.p: A council of senior Czech ministers has directed Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy to intensify final talks with Norway on a deal to diversify natural gas supplies away from solely Russian gas, a government spokesman said on Thursday.
Spokesman Ivo Strejcek told Reuters that Dlouhy was directed to "concentrate, above all, on price questions".
The Czech government has been considering four options for the diversification of gas supplies, and a decision has been expected since the beginning of the year.
The industry and trade ministry has said it was discussing four options for new gas supplies.
Strejcek nor ministry officials could say whether the Norwegian option would be the only diversification plan to move toward final consideration.
Dlouhy is scheduled to speak on the issue at a news conference this afternoon.
The four plans under consideration have been:

* Purchasing some Russian gas indirectly through Dutch company Nederlandse Gasunie NV, and Germany's Wintershall, a subsidiary of BASF . Gasunie would start supplies in 1998, delivering up to two billion cubic metres in 2005, with the agreement lasting until 2014. In case of a fall in Russian supplies, Gasunie would deliver its own gas through Wingas, a joint venture of Wintershall and Gazprom.

Wintershall offers a similar scheme, with deliveries through Wingas starting on January 1 next year, rising to one billion cubic metres in 2000, under a deal which would last until 2016. Negotiations with these firms are in the stage of initiating a supply contract. * Finalising an agreement for Norwegian gas, which has already had preliminary approval for supplies between 1997-2017. * A limited purchase from Mobil Europe Gas Inc , Germany's Brigitta Erdgas und Erdoel (BEB) and British Gas Plc. * Purchasing all gas from Russia's Gazprom using two different shipping routes, with a long-term agreement until 2016 and price guarantees until 1998.
The Czech Republic consumes around eight to nine billion cubic metres of gas per year, but volumes are expected to rise to some 12-13 billion cubic metres by the turn of the century.
